at last evening's benefit, given by Mr.
Silas Krum, manager of the Metropolitan
rink, to the Columbia Relief Association,
and which was held in that handsome
building. The attendance was large, but
not so large as was expected or desired,
but the men who were present had delight-
ful time, for the grand march was fine,
while the rendition of Strauss' difficult
"Fairies Moonlight Revels," literally
brought down the house to speak. It
was excellently played. It was the whole last
one of the most musical evenings ever
enjoyed by them.

Market Master George Briner, staunch
Democrat, a few days ago sent fine bas-
ket of fruit to Gov. Cleveland and yester-
day he received personal letter from the
president elect, acknowledging the pres-
ent and warmly thanking him for the
generous present.

It is reported that the furnaces of the works
have reduced the wages of its employes;
it is untrue, the furnaces are in good con-
dition, having recently received se-
orous orders enough to keep the men working
over winter. Heavy shipments of iron are
daily being made.

Farmers are erecting an elevator,
their ice houses at the works, which is
known as an endless chain elevator. The
chains when worked under the aid of
a steam engine travels 100 feet per minute, and
it moves two TONS of ice an hour; the ice
house holds about four TONS of ice and can
be supplied by the use of the elevator in one
week. Heretofore it required four weeks
of hard work to fill. A visit to the ice
house will convince persons that the
elevator is a success.

to meet on the second hour, in the old
"A SPY" building, in Bank alley, on Sunday
at 8, when and where a brakemen's
union will be organized.

week, from a stroke of apoplexy. He
leaves eight children. His remains will be
interred in Kinderhook on Sunday.

No. 2, will be held in the Vigilant parlor
on Tuesday, December 10th, 1884. The
following gentlemen will manage the
affair: Master of ceremonies, Franz
Stooker; floor managers, A. V. Rogers.

back word that he will never touch a penny of the
money until he has had justice done him in another
way. Thomas Conroy, now fifty years of age, was
born in the province of Leinster, Ireland, where the
firm of Conroy Brothers had a monopoly of supply-
ing bread and liquor to soldiers in the barracks
near Dublin. Michael Conroy, one of the firm, was
Thos. Conroy's father, and the other member of the
firm was Thomas Conroy, an uncle. When young
Thomas Conroy was 10 his father died. His mother
had been dead some years. His father left a will
directing that when Thomas became of age he
should be paid whatever the amount of the inter-
est of the deceased man in the supply business was.
Young Conroy took up his residence with his uncle
Thomas in Dublin. The young man was well edu-
cated of the higher class. There was another uncle named
Patrick who had married a woman who was be-
neath him in social standing; his wife's sister had
asked that he would be pleased to have his nephew
Thomas marry this niece. When it was proposed
it aroused the enmity of his uncle Patrick thereby,
and the latter sought means to revenge himself on
his nephew. The Molly Maguires, which originated in Ireland, were very strong
there. Their lawless acts had stricken terror into
the people. Patrick Conroy determined
to use this order to retaliate on his nephew, and
learned that his nephew was connected with the
criminals. Thomas was not only a member of the Molly
Maguires, but that he was secretary and book
keeper. A number of outrages had been per-
petrated in Dublin about that time, which had
been traced to this very lodge, and the elder
uncle called on him and accused him of being a
liar. This aroused the blood of young Conroy,
who was strongly opposed to the order of which
he was charged with being a member, and,
at the word of his uncle, Patrick, the young man
denounced him as liar and a villain. Thomas
was not to be spoken to in disrespectful language or to leave the house forever.

maintain another moment among flesh and blood that
had so belied him, and left the house. With it
he went to live in Calncoon, on the Erie railway, and
young Conroy hunted him up from there. He went
on a walk to New Orleans, where he had a friend. In
passing through the village of Mount Pleasant, in
this county, he stopped at the shop of a
shoemaker. He became so interested in it that he asked the
shoemaker if he did not want an apprentice. The
shoemaker did, and young Conroy went to work.


When Conroy came of age he received notice
from his uncle that he was entitled to $5,000 from
their business, and that it awaited his order. He
sent back the word he has sent every year since
that when they apologized to him and confessed
they had wronged him by the charges they made
against him in Ireland, he would go to Ireland and
claim the money, and never before. When Conroy
learned his trade he married Miss Delaney and
went to work for himself at Tanners Falls. He is
obliged to work hard and constantly to support
himself and family, and yet he will not break the
vow he took, when he left his native land to never
visit it again or touch one penny of the wealth he
was entitled to until his uncles confessed to him
that they had wronged him.

These figures will help us to realize something of the situation as to population. Between Philadelphia and New York Bishop Coke and his companions found a wilderness, the country population increasing in density as he left Philadelphia. This glance affords some estimate of the country at to this time.

But we may inquire as to what they foresaw of these times. To the extent they were able to look forward and see something of the history made during the century, they were excited by enthusiastic expectations. American Independence—the birth of a nation—was an event calculated to lift the veil a little, and lead to speculations of coming greatness; and however impossible it may have been to imagine the actual progress, yet very much less doubtless, seemed wonderful. The growth of the nation was an opportunity for church growth, and just as we derive no little inspiration from what we believe and hope, so, we do not doubt, they found an elation, born of religious confidence and zeal, which made them feel as if they stood upon a great stage, actors in affairs which had world wide significance.

But we must take account of their religious enthusiasm, especially in order to estimate the importance of this meeting. They had religious character and experience of a high order. They could encounter the perils of the ocean and the wilderness, and sing and shout the praise of God whatever the tempest might be—to ford rivers, or to pillow their heads upon a stone, if need be, were hardships not feared, nor thought of as reasons why their travels should be deferred. Such men, under such divine and gracious influences, confiding fully in divine leadership, anticipating great triumphs, halting in the wilderness to settle some matters of organization and form, may excite our admiration and account largely for our spiritual and wonderful heritage.

As we read of the greeting Coke received from Asbury, we cannot doubt the embrace and kiss were begotten of religious fervor, more than courtesy or any ordinary feeling of welcome. As soon as the time admitted they addressed themselves to the work. Garrettson was despatched hither and thither to inform the preachers of the Christmas Conference, and work was laid out for Coke and Asbury, and at once they went to the churches and from church to church, preaching the everlasting Gospel.

Six weeks thus spent together and then they met the preachers of the American Methodist Church. The number was not large, only sixty being present. Before they left Barratt's Chapel, we may suspect they had estimated the character of the gathering at the Christmas Conference, and the spirit of the men who were its members. We may be sure that Asbury's itinerant interviews with the preachers enabled him to appreciate their sentiments on ecclesiastical, as well as other subjects.

It was agreed, says Asbury, to form ourselves into an Episcopal Church, and to have superintendents, elders and deacons. Travellers in Europe frequently see
women carrying heavy burdens or drawing
great loads upon the public highway. We
are beginning to observe the same thing
occasionally. in America, such things are
shocking to the American sense OF fitness.


While women, under stress of poverty,
must work tor their livelihood, and while
all honor should be given to those who
cheerfully and bravely accept abnormal
conditions and bend their backs to the
wheel, society should save them from that
kind Of employment which compels them
to assume, in public view. the character
of beasts Of burden. The spectacle that
is tolerated among the European peasant
nv ought not to be suffered in this country.
The fact that the women who are thus
abused make no complaint has nothing to
do with the prophecies OF the matter. In
the streets of the large cities one does not
have 10 wander far before coming upon
a woman scavenger toiling under sack
Of refuse, or a woman CLEANER OF Goals and
sticks bending under the weight Of
picked-up fuel. In the country districts,
now and then, as the train-passenger is
whirled past farms and gardens, he catches
a glimpse OF a woman holding pillow or
welding hoe. The man who contem-
plates the spectacles without regret is out
Of place among true Americans. His ma
ture must be essentially brutal; selfish
ness rules in his heart and his mind is dis
posed to the oppression Of the weak.
Such men have eongenial existence only
where tyrants flourish and where they may
become the willing instruments of subject
grinding despots. :,


The day OF the knight-errant who found
his keenest inspiration in the defense of
his lady-lov has passed. but there is a
present demand for that higher chivalry
which preserves woman from the necessi-
ty for that work which the Indian warrior
assigns 10 his patient, enduring, slave-like
sauaw. The point is sometimes made
against those who are seeking to place the
ballot in the hands Of women, that on ac
cepting such favor they must necessarily
consent, at least by implication, to carry
muskets in time Of war. 1t is an abomi
nable proposition, shameful to those who
suggest it, The question of woman's
suffrage must be decided upon a broader
and better principle than that. The very
tact that such suggestion is made gives
occasion for the admonition that society
take care lest it shall permit the working
woman to be rated according to muscular
capabilty. We don't want to see women
digging. carrying mortar, throwing sledg-
es. pushing wheelbarrows, lifting bales,
and similar work. Great progress has
been made in opening avenues for the
employment of women, but let not the
time come when the sight of woman
working for bread shall become so com
mon that society will neglect to distin-
guish between that which she should do
and that from which she should be saved.
We must not grow used to seeing women
toilng in the streets. We must not grow
used to seeing them struggling under
heavy loads. We must not grow used to
the men who allow their mothers, wives
and daughters to do such work as Nature
never intended Such employment is a
retrogression to the savage state.


1t might be asked, what is the differ
ence between the lot of woman who
scrubs a floor, and that of another who
carries n pack through the streets as a
common laborer An immense difference
to the woman's personality and in moral
effect. Upon these nice distinctions the
tone of society depends. We must not
become so utterly practical that we may
disregard the sentiment of things all to-
gether. When the chivalric quality is
dulled. society drops back towards selfish
ness. Difference To woman is one of the
most conspicuous attributes OF the natur-
nj gentleman. And when a man can re-
gard with indifference or satisfaction. a
woman drawing a wagon upon which her
husband reCines. or hitched with n don
key to n cart as is SO often seen among the
European peas1ntry, or doing any manner
q! work like this, that man has become a
vicious element in American society.
That such spectacles are comparatively
rare in this country. as yet, is an agreed
BILE reflection, but they are not so rare
that protest is uncalled for, If the
women who thus work are of foreign
birth. and take such employment as a
matter of course, society owes ii not the
less to them than to itself to show them
better ways of earning a living.

and daughters to do such work as Nature
never intended. Such employment is a
retrogression to the savage state.

ence between the lot of woman who
scrubs a floor, and that of another who
carries a pack through the streets as a
common laborer? An immense difference
to the woman's personality and in moral
effect. Upon these nice distinctions the
tone of society depends. We must not
become so utterly practical that we may
disregard the sentiment of things all to-
gether. When the chivalric quality is
dulled, society drops back towards selfish-
ness. Difference to woman is one of the
most conspicuous attributes of the natur-
al gentleman. And when a man can re-
gard with indifference or satisfaction, a
woman drawing a wagon upon which her
husband reclines, or hitched with a don-
key to a cart as is so often seen among the
European peasantry, or doing any manner
of work like this, that man has become a
vicious element in American society.
That such spectacles are comparatively
rare in this country, as yet, is an agreed
reflection, but they are not so rare
that protest is uncalled for. If the
women who thus work are of foreign
birth, and take such employment as a
matter of course, society owes it not the
less to them than to itself to show them
better ways of earning a living.

to condense in the experience of few hours in
this city of Boston what otherwise I could not
have hoped to gain by over a year of travel. For
here in this historic hall, and in this illustrious
city rich in traditions of patriotic self sacrifice
and devotion, it is my peculiar good fortune to
meet in this inspiring arena an assemblage of
men representing every State and Territory of
this Union—an assemblage of men, the national
leaders of the Irish race on the American conti-
nent—men qualified by public service, by char-
acter, and by capacity, to interpret the thoughts
and utter the sentiments Of the Irish race upon
this great continent.


Ladies and gentlemen will say that I am
here not only as a delegate of the Irish parlia-


[Applause]; that I am here to speak to the peo-
ple Of America, not only on behalf
of that party which faces the oppressor of our
country on the floor of the House Of Commons,
but also to utter the sentiments of that organ-
ization which trains and organizes the resolu-
tion, the ingenuity and strength of the Irish
people for a struggle upon the soil of Ireland.
[Applause.] I am here as a representative of
united Ireland [Great applause and cheers].
I am here to say that there is no
difference in principle, no difference in intention
between the men who confront the oppressors Of
our country in the legislative arena and the men
who conduct public cause at home; and while
I declare that there is at this moment perfect
identity of action, perfect unity Of principle be-
tween the people in Ireland and we who struggle
for them in the English House of Commons, I
believe I may add that no man
who at this moment commands the CON-
fidence and love of the Irish people
will be found in the critical future, which is
near approaching, which will decide not only the
social but the political rights of our race to im-
pose any personal view or preference of his own
if he finds it will have the effect of injuring the
unity of the people or endangering the success
Of their cause. [Applause.] Speaking
to you, then, as the spokesman
of united Ireland, I would say that I have con-
fidence you will prove, on this occasion, that the
Irish race, long schooled in political adversity,
has learned to extract from it sweet results and
that, looking back upon the past of our country,
disfigured by the track of oppression and of
suffering, you will resolve that the historian
will not have it to say that
you added to those landmarks by your disunion,
but that you will reflect in your conclusions
here that unity to which the people at home
have been driven, and that whatever conclus-
ion you may come to will be the conclusion of you
all, and that whatever step YOU MAY take
to strike down the power of the oppressor,
that step you will take all together, and that there
shall be no disunion in your ranks [Great AP-
plause].


Mr. William Redmond, Jr., was next intro-
duced as former visitor in America, and was
received with much applause. He also made an
address, and was followed by Mrs. Parnell who
spoke a few words of cheer.


The committee on permanent organizatio n
reported Mr. Cannon of Iowa, for
president. DR. O'Reilly, Of Detroit,
then presented his report, showing total
receipts of $4,000. The committee on resolu-
tions asked that the platform be submitted to
Sexton and Redmond before being presented to
the convention, and it was so ordered. Ad-
journed until tomorrow.

His book is still peculiarly accounted a German classic. It retains that distinction solely by virtue of its style, and it has long ceased to be accepted by students as an authority. It is well known that Mr. Motley had hoped to supplement his story of the Dutch uprising for religious and civil liberty with an account of the great contest between Protestants and Catholics upon the wider field of Germany, but he was only able to complete what might be considered an introduction to such work in his description of the part played by Barneveld. Meanwhile the importance of more thorough acquaintance with the causes, incidents and results of the tremendous struggle, which began in 1618 with the revolt of Bohemia against Ferdinand of Austria, and ended thirty years later with the Peace of Westphalia, is more and more generally recognized. black ant, are able to destroy speedily
any kind of woodwork. They can
honeycomb big log till it may be
crushed by the pressure of hand.

ants have eaten everything but the

wood but teak; and through this they
bore, with the precision and smoothness

supposed to have been originally
brought there from one of the East
Indian islands-have cost hundreds of
thousands of dollars, and, though large
rewards have been offered for the dis
covery of means to exterminate them,
no remedy has yet been found.

Mr. Vanderbilt's Nautilus and Mr. Gould's
Atalanta, the cabins will be forward, and the
old-time quarter deck will be given up to the
seamen. The engines are to be placed about
amidships. Below deck, and just forward of
the engines, the main saloon will begin,
running the full width of the vessel, and is
to be lighted by an immense skylight, to be
finished in solid hard wood, and to be fur
nished with the richest material, including
sofas, chairs, and long extension table for
dining purposes. Leading from this
saloon is to be a hallway. Opening
from it, on the starboard side, is to be the
owners stateroom, a large room luxuriously
furnished. Just forward is another state
room, and opposite on the port side, three
staterooms for guests. At the end of the hall
way is to be a cabin for ladies, extending,
like the main saloon, across the vessel. For
ward of the cabin will be two rooms for the
maids. The furnishing of these rooms is to
be in hard wood.

One of the main rooms is to be the lounging
room or observation room, or whatever it
may be called, in the deck house. This is
reached by companionway from the hall
below. The stairs are to be of polished brass,
with mahogany railings, and the deck room
is to be finished in mahogany, with white
pine overhead and fresco work. Aft of this
deck saloon, with its magnificent appoint
ments, is to be a chart room finished in the
same manner.

All the officers and seamen are to be quar-
tered aft of the machinery. First comes a
galley on the starboard side, with rooms for
cooks, stewards, and engineers across the
passage on the port side. Aft of these are
the rooms of the mates, captain, and quarter
masters, and at the end of the passage is the
ward room. In the extreme stern of the
yacht ten seamen and as many seamen can
be quartered.

There will be more room in the Nourmahal
than in the Atalanta. It is expected that the
yacht will do well under canvas. The stand
ing rigging is to be of charcoal galvanized
wire and the running rigging of manila bolt
rope. The tall foremast, raking aft, will float
pennant 100 feet above the deck. Electric
bells from all the forward cabins and state
rooms will summon attendants and the elec
tric light will be used in every portion of the
yacht.

It is expected that Mr. Astor can take a trip
in his splendid craft, fitted and equipped in
every detail, before the hot weather of
August sets in. About three months will be
required to complete everything after the
launch.

The Republican County Convention
held in Arlington.


The meeting was fairly attended every town
represented except Poultney.


Thomas Bronsill of Poultney was elected
chairman and JOHN CURTIS of Bennington,
secretary.


There was considerable division in regard
to candidates, in the difficulty of selecting
a candidate throughout the shire, so no
candidate was nominated at that time.


From the south shire the names of Hon.
J. V. Carney of Remington and Thomas
J. Gardner of Poultney were presented for
senators. Mr. Carney was elected by a
handsome majority. From the north
shire the names of J. Q. Martin of Man-
chester, and John Curtis of Dorset, were
presented. The canvass had been vig-
orously pressed by the friends of both, and
the result before the vote was taken was
doubtful. Mr. Martin had many strong
friends who urged his eminent fitness for
the office, while his opposers claimed with
much force that he was prominently iden-
tified with the contest two years ago,
which would have a tendency to lessen his
vote if nominated. The ballot resulted
in 81 votes for Curtis and 20 for Martin.
On motion of Mr. Martin's friends the
nomination of Mr. Curtis was made upon
motion.


There was not much contest for the
other places on the ticket and Thomas
J. Gardner of Poultney and W. S. Bentley of
Sandgate were nominated for Assistant
Judges. Jas. L. McCall of Rupert for
sheriff. Ed. L. Bates of Bennington for
States Attorney. S. H. Crum of Sunder-
land for High Bailiff, L. L. Sibbs of Ben-
nington and L. Munson of Manchester,
Judges of Probate for their respective
districts.


The following gentlemen were elected
county committee: Loveland Munson,
Wm. H. Bradford, E. G. Woodwork, A.
H. Potter and Wm. P. Madison.


Col. Colburn of the committee on reso-
lutions presented the following which
were adopted:


Resolved, That the Republicans of Ben-
nington county in convention assembled
do approve the platforms of the National
Republican and State Conventions, and
heartily indorse the candidates by them
nominated.


Resolved, That we recognize the im-
portance of the great National contest
now pending, on the prosperity and wel-
fare of the country, and that it is the duty
of every patriotic citizen to be at the polls
at the September election.


Resolved, That we present the candi-
dates this day put in nomination as worthy
of hearty support and bespeak for them
full vote at the polls.


The ticket as a whole is a strong one
and will receive, at least, the full Republi-
can vote. Judge Carney, the candidate for
senator from the south shire, is well
known as a man of integrity and more
than ordinary ability. John Curtis, the
candidate from the north shire, is not so
well known, but is a man of liberal educa-
tion, having graduated at the Vermont U-
niversity, is thoroughly posted on current
events, is a man of spotless integrity, a
straight Republican who has never sought
office, a man of the soundest judgement,
and a man who, if he had devoted his life
to political life, instead of civil,
would long ago have made his
mark, and we will believe make a good
senator.


Jas. L. McCall, candidate for sheriff,
has had more experience as deputy than
any other man in the county. He is a man
of integrity and worthy of hearty support.


T. L. Bates, candidate for States Attor-
ney, is a bright young lawyer, popular in
the community where he resides, and we be-
lieve is competent to fulfill the duties of
the office to general satisfaction.
The other candidates are all good men
and worthy of support, and we have no doubt
all will be elected with at least the usual
Republican majority.

The Opera House last evening held as large
and fine an audience as has been seen in that
place of amusement this season. The event
was a notable one; It was the presentation of
Shakespeare's grand tragedy "Hamlet" by
home talent, under the direction of Mr. Ed.
ward Larkin, with that gentleman in the lead
role. For the healing of the sufferers of the
great flood of '84 for several months past,
ladies and gentlemen whose names appear
in the cast given below, have been hard at
work studying their parts. The result shown
last night was a remarkably good amateur
performance; one that reflected great
credit on each and every one. The parts were
elegantly dressed; no Shakespearean play ever
presented here was better costumed, all were
well up in their lines and the play throughout
worked very smoothly. This is saying a
great deal when it is remembered that the
players are not professionals and that this
was their first public appearance in the play.
The cast was as follows:

Mr. Edward Larkin as Hamlet
King Claudius of Denmark, Mr. Geo. Martin
Polonius, Claudius, M. J. Scharkler
Laertes, Friend of Hamlet, Mr. Evan F. Darlin

First Actor, Mr. Howard Keen
Second Actor, Mr. Martin Iron
Ophelia, Miss House

character he appeared in, as well with regard
to Hamlet as the embodiment of metaphysical
speculation, as in his regard to the
other parts. His presentation has, over that
of many professional stars, this conspicuous
merit: that in right places Hamlet is kept at
the front, and again in right places he is
given due subordination. The obvious re-
sult of this is to give to each player an op-
portunity to do his best in his part and to
treat it with the importance which
the dramatist attaches to it, be the same much
or little. Mr. Larkin has grace of posture
and of movement, a great merit in any actor.
He is so much in love with the play as well
as with his own part, that he gives great at-
tention to every detail, sacrificing nothing
to the general purposes for the sake of his
own personal success.

The close study which he has given to the
part and play is evident from the time he
had his first appearance until his final exit.
He has a fine sense of every situation which
would become still more apparent upon ex-
tended experience. His voice is good and
more cultivation will make it better. He
might easily avoid the prolonged
head tones which take from the
voice the power to command vol-
ume and to shade with nice discrimins-
ton. His reading in many places is almos-
t essentially his own—that is not necessarily
a demerit. Much the same may be said of
his business, mechanical movements, atti-
tudes, and the like—and this, too, imparts

impersonation of a much done part.

Ophelia, and in the conclusion of the final
scene, his voice shows a fine sympathetic
quality and his action is suited to the word.

Hamlet that it is also Shakespeare's Hamlet;
that it has dignity, subtlety, some power and
a gentle finish, all of which are noticeably good
qualities, study and practice would improve.

Captain Hetherington, whose apiaries along the Cherry Valley Creek, in Schoharie county, annually turn out over 100,000 pounds of the choicest honey, takes nine men and two steam saw-mills five weeks to prepare the lumber for the boxes in which the honey is made by his bees. Nearly 150,900 panes of glass about six inches square are used in these boxes. Captain Hetherington has at work this season nearly 2,500 swarms of bees. These are not all on his own premises, but are scattered among the orchards and fields of farmers along the creek, to whom he pays a rent for the privilege of his bees working in the clover, buckwheat, or whatever blossoms are in season on the farms. The care of these bees does not fall to the owner of the land. Captain Hetherington keeps men and teams constantly employed looking out for them. He has received as much as $25,600 for one season's crop.


Another large New York State bee-keeper is C. B. Isham, of Peoria. Up to 1879 there was no market in England for American honey. The English dealers would not handle it, and the periodicals devoted to the interests of bee keepers in that country cried it down in every possible way. The reason for this was that they knew the superiority of American honey, both in flavor and appearance over the British article, and were aware that if it was once introduced in London, it would be a great blow to the trade in the home supply. There was a smart Yankee named Hoge working for grocery in this city, and he assured his employers that, if they would give HIM the commission, he would manage to place American honey on the English market. A large lot of Isham's honey, which the firm was then handling, was packed, just as it came from the hives, and Hoge was sent to London with it. He found he needed all his Yankee ingenuity and acuteness, for he met with universal opposition among the dealers. He labored with them for weeks to no purpose. In conversation one day with the proprietor of the hotel at which he stopped, the latter told Hoge that if he could manage to have his honey introduced on the table of Queen Victoria it would solve the problem at once, for if she was pleased with it she would communicate to Hoge through the Lord Steward. This communication once made public would make American honey the fashion in England.


A former Lord Steward was a friend of the hotel keeper and was at that time engaged largely in the manufacture and sale of pickles. This man the landlord introduced to Hoge. They dined together. Hoge gave the pickle man an immense order for his goods, to present to the American grocer. More wine followed and before the ex-Lord Steward went away he promised to use his influence to have the American honey introduced on the royal table. He succeeded in inducing the then Lord Steward, Sir John Cowell, to accept a box of the honey for the Queen, and to serve it on her table. The Queen was so delighted with the honey that she directed the Lord Steward to present her thanks to the donor, to order a supply of ten cases at once and to keep American honey constantly on the royal table.


Hoge lost no time in making this communication public. The consequence was that the opinion of American honey changed at once, and Hoge came back to New York secretly laughing at the Britishers, but rejoicing over an order for 5,000 pounds of American honey for the English market, which he carried in his pocket. The demand for it has increased ever since, and the trade that was started in New York State honey is now largely shared by the California product.


In California there are no long winters, with dearth of flowers through which bees must be fed by artificial means, and in the mouth of almost every canyon there is a bee ranch or apiary. The bee-keeper of the Pacific coast is not beset by as many difficulties as confront his Eastern brother, and he grows indolent and rich from the labor of his ever-industrious brown-winged servants. These bee ranches are models of neatness and comfort, and the business is so light, pleasant and profitable, and requires so little capital at the start, that it is fast becoming the leading industry in many localities on the coast. You see men, women and children who own extensive bee ranches, among them being many who are physically unable to attend to business requiring active superintendence. There is a constant buzzing of wings in these canyons, caused by the endless goings and comings of the bees, and the burden of honey they carry collectively is so great that the air is perpetually filled with the fragrance of the fields.


"Why do we never see red clover honey advertised?" asked reporter.


"For the simple reason that there is never any made by honey bees. There is no blossom so rich in stores of sweetness as the red clover blossom, as every schoolboy whose privilege it is to pluck them and suck their nectar knows. But the honey bee never collects it, because it cannot. The corolla tube of the red clover is so deep and small that the bee cannot reach the honey. The bee knows this and if you will think a moment, you will remember that you never saw a hive bee on a red clover blossom. They do not waste their time in efforts to obtain sweets that are beyond their reach. But the humble bee levies tribute on every red clover field in his bailiwick. As smart as the hive bee is, it has yet to learn the trick that is as old as the hills of its gigantic and more stupid-seeming cousin. When the humble bee lights on a head of red clover he punctures a hole in the base of the corolla, and, thrusting in his tongue, sucks out the nectar. Unfortunately this big, clumsy bee is not much of a honey maker. You might rob a score of humble bee nests and not obtain a quarter of a pound of honey; and besides, his nests are few and far between. Consequently we will have to wait until the hive bee learns to drill into the blossom to get the nectar before we can have red clover honey for our waffles."

Chief Naval Constructor Theodore A. Viton, chief of the bureau of construction and repairs, in his annual rep't recommends a specific appropriation of $1,911,900 for the seven new steel cruisers recommended by the [Board]. He recommends the completion of the New York, on the stocks at the Brooklyn navy yard, and the building of two composite, barque rigged, light-sparred Clippers built of 5,000 tons, with auxiliary steam power, to cost $1,500,000, to take the place of the Jamestown, Portsmouth and Saratoga ironclad ships the latter vessels being unfit for repairs after this year; six new steel monitors Amphitrite, Monadnock, Puritan and Terror, at a cost of $1,113,651 as he deems them the best type of vessel in existence for coast and harbor defense, and they are as good as any afloat anywhere. It will take a year to complete them after authority of Congress is obtained but when finished we would have five, the Monitor Monadnock being the other splendid harbor defense iron-clads that could be sent to distant points if required. Plans are being prepared for an 800 ton cruiser, two heavily armed gunboats, one armed dispatch boat, one light cruising gunboat, and one armed ram.

Commodore Wilson says that with the exception of a few improved tools required for the preparation of plates, beams, and angles, and the erection of furnaces for heating angle iron, and plates, there is no private establishment in this country which has better facilities for steel ship building than can be found in the navy yards, and few indeed which can compete with them in all respects. At present there are but few private establishments in the country, and but one navy yard which could commence and carry on with any degree of rapidity the building of steel ships. In order to meet any trouble which may arise in the future, and which all nations are liable to, it seems that the wisest and certainly the most economical course for this government to pursue is to immediately equip its navy yards with the necessary tools and plant for building such steel armored or unarmored vessels as the necessities of the service may demand, and for this purpose the bureau has asked that it be assisted in this work by the appropriation of $160,000. In the event of an appropriation being made for more steel ships the bureau hopes that at least one half of the ships may be built in the navy yards in competition as to cost and character of work with outside establishments. Common sense patriotism requires that our navy yards should be put in first class condition of efficiency. Mr. Merrill is a man of wonderful constitution, but his age is against him in this fight. He is sixty-five years old.

The last paralytic stroke affected the muscles of his head and he was fighty for several days. This feature has been quite alarming. The sufferer is receiving the closest and best medical treatment the country affords, and his thousands of friends over the northwest still hope that he will finally master the aggravating and distressing disease that has attacked him.

Mr. Merrill is one of the best known rail-roaders in the country. He has been the general manager of the vast St. Paul system continually since 1865. ship Laxham, which collided with the Span
ish steamer Gijon, report that on the evening
of the collision there was thick fog. The
Laxham was going slow. Both steamers
were sounding their whistles. The Gijon
struck the Laxham amidships and the latter
was nearly cut asunder. The funnel fell
and the steam pipe burst. The chief engi-
neer was horribly scalded. Most of the Lax
ham's crew boarded the Gijon. The captain
of the Laxham tied his wife and child to
himself, and all three were hauled aboard
the Gijon. The Laxham sank in
twenty minutes after the collision.
Not long before the Gijon began
to settle terrible confusion prevailed. The
captain stood with revolver in his hand,
but was unable to keep order. The passen-
gers and crew were fighting for their lives.
Boats were lowered and filed to the gun
wales, but they could not accommodate half
the people. Those fortunate enough to se-
cure places in them were obliged to keep off
others with knives. The Gijon sank bow
first. The quarter deck was crowded with
men and women at the time. The captain
and officers were standing on the bridge. It
is estimated that 100 persons perished.

AN INTERESTING CASE.

LONDON, July 28.—The trial of the action
for damages by Mrs. Weldon against Mr.
Semple, the medical man who signed certif-
icate for her seclusion as "a person of un-
sound mind, and fit subject for care and
treatment" under which the attempt
was made to take her to lunatic
asylum, was concluded to-day. The
verdict in favor of Mrs. Weldon
for £50 was rendered. The trial took place
before Justice Hawkins of the court of the
queens bench and common jury. The de-
fendant was represented by able counsel, but
Mrs. Weldon conducted her own case. The
trial attracted much attention and the court
was thronged.

FRANCE AND GERMANY.

PARIS, July 28.—The Figaro has written a bitter
article declaring England never helped but
always thwarted France, her friendship was
false and the alliance with her hollow. The
Figaro advises France to abandon the rela-
tions with England, give up her prejudices
and hatred and make an alliance with Ger-
many. Germany was an honest enemy, and
she had been an honest ally.

ANTI-JEWISH OUTBREAK.

VIENNA, July 28.—Of the persons
concerned in the anti-Jewish out-
break at Zaleszczyky, the birthplace of Esther
Solomassy, the girl alleged to have been
killed by the Jews in connection with certain
religious rites, two have been condemned
to five years and one to four years imprison-
ment.

MISCELLANEOUS.

LONDON, July 28.—Gladstone stated this
evening in the commons that an important
point rose in the Egyptian conference to-day
which the delegates thought necessary to
refer to the home government. They ex-
pect reply tomorrow when a conclusion
will be speedily arrived at. All the dele-
gates are anxious to press matters to settle-
ment.

LONDON, July 28.—In the commons to-day
A. E. Ashley, under secretary of the colonial
department, stated the government was
ready to confirm the Queensland scheme for
a confederation of the Australian colonies
and the annexation of New Guinea and
other Pacific islands as soon as the colonies
determine upon the necessary steps.
PARIS, July 28.—The government decided,
a majority of the deputies concurring, to
abandon revising the powers of the senate
in relation to the budget. This will enable
the senate to pass the remainder of the
revision bill. The government organized
posts of sanitary supervision on the Lyons
railway and other lines.

MADRID, July 28.—Minister Foster had
another important interview Saturday with
Senior Castillo, the Spanish premier. It is a
difficult task for Spanish government to
reconcile the conflicting commercial inter-
ests of Peninsula and Cuba.

LONDON, July 28.—The Egyptian confer-
ence remained in session three hours and a
half and adjourned for a short meeting to-
morrow.

CHOLERA NEWS.

PARIS, July 28.—There were thirteen
deaths from cholera last night. At Toulon
there were fourteen. At Lavallette, village
near Toulon, there were four. Fugitives are
now prevented from returning to Toulon. A
strong wind from the northwest is prevailing
and the weather is cooler. The mortality is
decreasing in the cities but increasing in the
country among the peasants.

MARSEILLES, July 26.—There were five
deaths from cholera here since 8 o'clock this
morning.

ATHENS, July 28.—The steamer Tiger,
from Marseilles arrived off Piraeus yesterday
with two cases of cholera. Admittance to
the port was refused, and the steamer de-
parted for Smyrna.

BERLIN, July 28, it is stated that the run-
ning of through coaches on railways between
Germany and France will be stopped for fear
of cholera.

GLASGOW, July 28.—The steamer Clan
Machean, from Marseilles arrived to-day.
The medical examiner found no infection
and the crew in perfect health.

WASHINGTON, July 28.—Secretary Freling-
husen has just received a telegram from
Consul Mason at Marseilles as follows:

"There is marked improvement in Mar-
seilles and Toulon cholera deaths. From a
daily average of 80 it fell to 43 Wednesday,
45 Thursday, 80 Friday, 15 Saturday, 80 Sun-
day, and last night 10 in 11 hours. The mor-
tality in all cases is also declining. At Tou-
lon the average fell from 40 to 15. Insulated
cases are reported from various parts of the
district. The epidemic is declared severe at
Aries and AK.

The surgeon general of the Marine has received a
telegram from James H. Holt, president of
the Louisiana state board of health: Exhaustive
investigation fails to establish even a
remote suspicion of Asiatic cholera as the
cause of the death of the infant Picaliotos,
passenger on the Anna J. Silver.

poned.

Logan would bring to any cause which he espoused. Logan had been present at the battle the day before, but the others were not at that time aware of the fact. He had been the bitter and determined political foe of at least two of the most prominent men who constituted the little group. It seemed that some consultation had been going on among its members when the informant approached, for just at that moment Kellogg, glancing towards the retreating figure of the swarthy statesman and addressing Governor Yates said:

"Dick, I think one of us should speak to Logan."

Governor Yates looked toward the gloomy figure which by this time had turned its black browed, wrathful eyes toward them, and claimed:

"You can do so if you wish; I'll be—if I do."

A momentary silence ensued between the members of the little coterie, until Logan had made two or three more turns, when Kellogg stepped forward and addressed him:

"John," said he, "we want to know what you think about this matter."

Unionism and disunionism were so such absorbing topics at that time that it was not deemed necessary to specify what "matter" was alluded to, but it was not without a tremor of the voice that brave Kellogg put the question.

John Logan's hands dropped to his sides and he took three or four strides, which brought him in such close proximity to the little group that he could have touched either with an outstretched finger as he answered Kellogg in a voice which trembled with pity and anger:

"Bill, did you see that boy of McCook's killed yesterday?" "The boy of McCook's" was a seventeen-year-old son of Major McCook, father of the three Gems, McCooks, and had been killed at Bull Run the day before.

Kellogg, who had been a witness of his death, replied: "I did."

"And did YOU," said Logan, in a terrible voice, "see that internal scoundrel of a rebel lieutenant-general run him through the body with his sword when the poor wounded boy had his bleeding hands raised in pitiful appeal for quarter?"

"I did," said Kellogg.

"Well, so did I," said Logan, "and by the living God above us, I am from this time henceforth Abolitionist and enemy to a cause which sanctions such proceedings."

And then, turning to Yates, he continued:

"Yates, I am going home to raise a regiment. Will you give me commission?"

"GLADLY and cheerfully, John."

And in this way did John A. Logan enter upon that other phase in his great career, which will be so fittingly rewarded on the 4th of November.

STORY OF THEIR LIVES—A MEETING AT

PLYMOUTH CHURCH

A small audience gathered in Plymouth Church yesterday afternoon at the church. Messrs. Mabee and English were present, conducting in Brooklyn this week. They ascended the platform with their assistants, W. F. Burnett, Mrs. Burnett and Miss Hillis. Mrs. Burnett played small organ and Miss Burnett accompanied the voices with choruses.

After several Gospel hymns had been sung, Mr. English related his personal experience. He is a man of about forty years of age, of medium height, slim, and quick in speech. He was dressed in a clerk's business suit and a gold pendant glittered on his watch chain. He spoke with great volubility and without much change of inflection, save at certain points in his narrative when the sudden change was startling. Many of the ordinary set phrases of temperance workers and revivalists were therefore in use. In substance he said:

"I have been disenthralled by the grace of God from the power of strong drinks. I was when I was ten, when I was fourteen years old, I had had enough to die in school, and all my lifetime. I was in the camp for troops, but my father would not let me go until I was sixteen. I joined the New York Harris Light Cavalry, under him who afterward became General George A. U.S. Army. I went to the oil regions which were the scene of great excitement, and mingled in much sin. I went back to my home in Fort Plain, and on January 7, 1871, took my last breath. I was saved by a helping hand in Lancaster. I was further removed in 1873 when death came to me. I went to the house of Mrs. John A. Kerr, and her illustrations that reclaimed me have led me to the pledge and I have hope of life eternal. We business in this work in this work are in God's service. Those who can see us reformed now are the ones who formerly called us drunkards and had doubt rather than confidence in reformed men. The red ribbon taxing us and throwing them on the desk is a sign to not drink now, whether we ever have or not."

He added, though religious, and wholly non-partisan, he believes in both legal and moral causes of temperance work, the former for the drunkard and the latter for the liquor seller. Both are needed in contending for the great moral principle to save the man from sinking in wretchedness and try to make a man of him. No one feels his degradation more than a drunkard.

Joseph Patrick English then made a brief speech, being ten years older than Mr. Mabee and was born in Ireland. He was formerly an actor and a liquor seller in Poughkeepsie. After he reformed he kept a tailor shop. It is only recently that he devoted his whole time to temperance work. At the American Temperance Union meeting in Chickering Hall there was an unusually full musical programme. Joseph A. Bogardus presided. Mr. Field Sears was the first speaker, and said in part:

"The liquor question pressing itself and making itself felt never before. Business men and philanthropists have taken hold of the question well as reformers.
